title: Breaking the \(2^{n}\) barrier for weighted TSP
formal: Do there exist constants \(\varepsilon \in (0,1), c\ge 1\) and a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every complete undirected graph on \(n\ge 3\) labelled vertices with nonnegative binary-encoded integer edge weights of total encoding length L, outputs a minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle with probability at least \(2/3\) in worst-case time \(O((2- \varepsilon )^{n}(n+\mathrm{L})^{c})\)?
definitions: Each unordered pair of distinct vertices has one explicitly listed weight. A Hamiltonian cycle visits each vertex exactly once before returning to its first vertex, and its weight is the sum of its n edge weights. Output the cyclic list of vertex labels. The input has no metric, bounded-weight, planarity or sparsity promise. Use a random-access word RAM with \(w=B\lceil n+\log _{2}(\mathrm{L}+2)\rceil\) bits per word for one fixed sufficiently large integer B; unit-cost operations are reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\) and integer division by nonzero words. Integers occupying several words incur the cost of all word operations. This word size permits addressing exponential-space subset tables; its polynomial bit-operation overhead is already permitted by the polynomial factor in \(n+\mathrm{L}\). The running-time bound includes reading weights, preprocessing, random bits and output and holds on every execution. Only independent private fair random bits are allowed; there is no quantum access, advice or oracle. The constants \(\varepsilon ,c,B\) and the implicit multiplicative constant are independent of n,L and the weights. A deterministic algorithm also qualifies. Dependence polynomial in the numerical maximum weight, rather than its binary length, does not qualify.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
why: Locate the fundamental exponential-time cost of exact weighted routing beyond the long-standing subset barrier.

importance.reason: A central exact-algorithm question with a sixty-year base-two barrier and a modern improvement that carefully distinguishes prefactor from exponent. It is separate from metric TSP approximation and from Hamiltonian-cycle detection.

progress.text: The Bellman and Held–Karp subset formulation gives the classical \(O(2^{n} n^{2})\) bound, recalled by the 2024 primary paper.

context_blocks.text: The exact travelling salesman problem asks for a cheapest tour through all vertices. In the general weighted setting, discovering a Hamiltonian cycle is not enough: the input is complete, so tours certainly exist, but their costs can vary greatly. The computational target is the minimum among them.

The classical subset dynamic program has a base-two dependence on the number of vertices. Stoian’s 2024 algorithm improves the familiar \(O(2^{n} n^{2})\) time by a factor \(2^{\Omega (\sqrt{\log  n})}\). Its bound retains the exponential base two and does not yield \(O*((2- \varepsilon )^{n})\) for any fixed positive \(\varepsilon\).

This distinction is substantial even though both bounds are exponential. A fixed base reduction saves an exponential factor on increasingly large instances, whereas savings in the polynomial or subexponential prefactor do not. The card asks about unrestricted classical algorithms, not about the optimality of the original dynamic-programming recurrence.

Weight encoding separates this target from several related exact questions. A method whose time is polynomial in the maximum integer weight can be very expensive when a large weight has a short binary representation. Likewise, faster algorithms for unweighted Hamiltonicity or for special weighted graph classes do not establish the general weighted guarantee.

No asserted reduction from SETH is built into the question. The desired algorithmic existence is itself the target; a conditional lower bound must state its assumption separately. The Parameterized and exact algorithms bucket is appropriate because the defining issue is the exponential dependence on n, rather than polynomial-time approximation of a tour.
